title: Blind Symmetry Matching in Quantum States with Application to Shot-Count Reduction
abstract: Measuring a quantum computation in a basis adapted to a symmetry it carries reduces the repeated measurements, commonly referred to as ``shots'', needed to read a statistical answer. Detecting the symmetry a quantum state carries has many uses: certifying a claimed symmetry, identifying a conserved-charge sector, flagging symmetry-breaking as an error signature, and selecting a compression or readout basis; shot-count reduction is developed here as one exemplary case. Existing methods assume the symmetry is known in advance; we remove that assumption. When it is unknown, the carried symmetry is discovered from the data by a symmetry test that scores candidate groups, and the largest passing group is exploited as the measurement basis. We state the pipeline precisely, prove the selection rule is unbiased, and charge discovery in full. Two conditions are treated, both detected by the same score with a different projection: a weak condition, commutation with the representation, and a strong condition, confinement to a single charge sector, the distinction drawn in the quantum-reference-frame literature. A single circuit, a controlled twirl followed by a SWAP test, discovers both: discarding the group register tests the weak condition, post-selecting it the strong one. The framework is general over finite groups, with cyclic (Fourier), dihedral, and symmetric-group (Schur-Weyl) examples; strong confinement to the symmetric, or Dicke, subspace is an exponential reduction. Seeded demonstrations show the loop wins net of discovery: weak matching on momentum readout reduces shots by a factor widening from ten to several thousand, and strong matching on a two-system target by a further factor of the subsystem size. Blind symmetry matching is a practical primitive for the common case where the matched basis cannot be written down in advance.
summary: This paper introduces Blind Symmetry Matching, an advanced technique to estimate unknown statistical properties in quantum computations by first discovering the underlying symmetry group from measurement data. By selecting and exploiting this discovered symmetry, the method significantly reduces the required number of measurements (shots) compared to structure-blind estimation techniques.
main_problem: To develop a method, called Blind Symmetry Matching, that reduces the required number of measurement shots for estimating unknown statistical quantities in quantum computations when the underlying symmetry is not known beforehand.
main_result: The proposed pipeline successfully discovers an unknown symmetry group and exploits it to achieve significant shot count reductions, with the strong confinement mode showing superior scaling ($\propto L^2$) compared to structure-blind methods.
method: The method involves a three-step process: (1) Discovery of candidate symmetries via specialized tests (weak/strong twirls), (2) Selection of the largest passing group ($G^\star$), and (3) Exploitation by measuring the target observable in the symmetry-adapted basis.
model_or_system: The framework is general over finite groups, demonstrated using quantum computations on systems like an L-site ring or two interacting systems. The target quantity to be estimated is a statistical expectation value of an operator $R$.
key_observables: Matching Score ($s_T(R)$), Shot Count Reduction Factor, Weak/Strong Twirl measurements.
important_parameters: System size ($L$), group order ($|G|$), and the ratio between discovery cost and exploitation savings.
main_assumptions: The target quantity must be statistical (an expectation value or distribution) rather than a single deterministic outcome. The discovery overhead must be less than the shot savings achieved by exploiting the symmetry.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall blind-matching pipeline (Discovery $	o$ Selection $	o$ Exploitation), detailing circuits for weak vs. strong twirls, and comparing scaling costs ($L^4$ vs $L^3$ vs $L^2$) across different modes.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of unknown symmetry estimation, details the mathematical framework involving weak (commutation) and strong (confinement) symmetry tests, proves the selection rule is unbiased, and concludes with seeded demonstrations showing exponential resource savings.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, general-purpose primitive for quantum algorithm design that moves beyond assuming prior knowledge of system symmetries, which is crucial for applying quantum computation to complex physical systems where symmetries are emergent or unknown.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The blind-matching pipeline. Discovery scores a candidate family by a symmetry test (weak twirl or strong sector projection), the selection rule takes the largest passing group, and exploitation reads the target in its symmetry- adapted basis. Here R is the unknown state, or its covariance, whose carried symmetry is to be discovered. Every shot, discovery included, is charged against the structure-blind baseline.

Fig. 2. The discovery circuit. A controlled group action twirls one copy of the target; discarding the group register C realizes the weak twirl (incoherent average), while post-selecting it on |+G⟩realizes the strong twirl (coherent average, heralded by the sector weight). The SWAP test on ancilla a returns the matching score. The controlled twirl and Hilbert-Schmidt test are in the symmetry-testing family of [8]; amplitude estimation accelerates the readout. For a cyclic group |+G⟩= H⊗n |0⟩and the controlled action is one modular adder.

Fig. 3. Weak-mode loop on momentum readout. (A) Discovery recovers the matched group from a few symmetry-test shots per candidate. (B) The structure-blind cost grows as L2 while the total pipeline cost stays nearly flat; discovery cost alone falls with L.

Fig. 4. Strong-mode loop on the two-system target. (A) The occupied sector is recovered from a handful of charge-measurement shots. (B) Structure- blind cost grows as L4, weak exploitation as L3, and strong discovery-plus- exploitation as L2; the strong mode buys an extra factor of L over the weak mode.
